title: Agreeing to an Operating Principle Before a Difficult Discussion or Debate
author: Admired Leadership
summary: This piece recommends securing agreement on a single shared operating principle before entering a difficult discussion, debate, or negotiation, arguing that shared values create common ground that reduces adversarial dynamics. It offers a menu of candidate principles — that the purpose is finding the best solution rather than winning, that old ground is off-limits, that either side could be wrong — and stresses that only one such principle needs to be agreed upon to set a cooperative tone. The essay closes by noting that if parties can't even agree to the operating principle itself, that failure is diagnostic and worth pausing on before attempting the substantive discussion at all.
points: Recommends securing agreement to a single shared operating principle before difficult discussions, rather than relying on general ground rules or agendas.
Distinguishes operating principles from procedural agendas or vague 'let's listen well' guidelines — principles are substantive commitments to a stance.
Offers a specific menu of candidate principles (seeking best solution not victory, no relitigating old ground, both sides could be wrong) leaders can propose.
Argues only one shared principle is needed to establish a cooperative tone for an entire discussion.
Treats a failure to agree even on the operating principle itself as diagnostic — a signal to reconsider whether the discussion should proceed at all.
quotes: Having one shared value that applies more precisely to any difficult discussion is a working principle that will guide the exchange.
That the purpose of the discussion is to find the best solution, not to win the argument. That covering old ground and reviewing past arguments is off-limits as a way to look forward.

By agreeing to an operating principle before launching into any discussion, debate, or negotiation, the parties begin with the tangible evidence that they can work together cooperatively without being disrespectful.
The team or parties need to agree to only one standard or precept to set the collaborative tone that will benefit them.
In the unusual event that the parties cannot agree to the working principle, the leader might consider the implications of attempting any discussion in such a moment.
